result:
Medieval scribes complained in the margins of their manuscripts, and I find this endlessly comforting.

Copying a book by hand took months. The work was cold, cramped, and hard on the eyes, and the monks who did it sometimes left small notes at the edges of the page. "Oh, my hand." "The ink is thin." "Thank God, it will soon be dark." One wrote, upon finishing, "Now I've written the whole thing; for Christ's sake give me a drink."

These were people producing some of the most beautiful objects of their age, sacred texts with gold leaf and impossible knotwork, and they were also bored, sore, and watching the window for dusk. Both things were true at once. The grandeur and the grumbling share a page.

My favorite is a ninth-century Irish monk who paused his scholarly work to write a poem about his cat, Pangur Bán. He compares the cat's hunting of mice to his own hunting of meaning: each of them absorbed in his craft, neither bothering the other. It may be the warmest thing ever written about working beside an animal. And in a fifteenth-century manuscript from Dubrovnik, a cat simply walked across the wet ink, leaving paw prints that survive to this day.

What moves me is how these small intrusions collapse the distance. History tends to hand us people as monuments, serious and finished. But the margins say otherwise. Someone's back hurt. Someone loved their cat. Someone wanted a drink. A thousand years on, the official text matters less to me than the human who leaked out around its edges.
